posts.title: What a phishing alert at 2am looks like
posts.excerpt: Most phishing alerts are quiet and dull. Here is how one is read, judged and closed on the night desk.
posts.content:
At 02:10 a mail gateway flags a message sent to the finance team of a client: an invoice from a supplier the firm has not used before. One of the two analysts on the desk opens it within minutes. Last year the median time from alert to a person looking at it was 11 minutes, and the aim is always to beat that.

What the analyst checks

  • Who sent it, and whether the sending domain was registered last week
  • Whether the link goes where the text says it goes
  • Whether anyone has already opened it or signed in through it

In this case the link leads to a copy of a Microsoft 365 sign-in page. Nobody has clicked. The analyst blocks the sender for the whole firm, pulls the message out of the three mailboxes it reached and writes a short note.

What the client sees

Nothing at 02:10. In the morning report there is one paragraph: what arrived, that no one had opened it, and what we did. If someone had entered a password, the desk would have disabled the account and called the named contact straight away.

Most alerts are not like this. We close the majority as harmless and say so, because a report full of drama helps nobody. The point of the night desk is that when the real one comes, a person is already awake.

posts.title: Backups that actually restore
posts.excerpt: A backup you have never restored is a hope. Three small checks that turn it into a plan.
posts.content:
Almost every small firm has a backup. Far fewer have ever restored from it. During onboarding we ask one question: when did you last get a file back? The silence that follows is the most useful part of the visit.

Three checks worth doing

  • Restore one real file and one whole folder each quarter, and write down how long it took
  • Keep one copy somewhere an attacker on your network cannot reach or delete
  • Make sure every server and the laptops that matter are on the list, not just the main file server

Ransomware attackers know about backups. They look for them first, and they try to delete or encrypt them before they announce themselves. A copy that is always connected and always writable can be lost along with everything else.

What we do about it

The desk checks every night that your backups finished, and flags a job that failed or shrank suspiciously. In onboarding, Priya Nair restores a sample with you, so you know what a good restore looks like and who does it at 03:00.

None of this is exciting. That is the idea. The week a friend of our founder lost to ransomware in 2014 would have been an afternoon if a tested backup had been waiting.

posts.title: MFA fatigue: when the phone will not stop buzzing
posts.excerpt: Multi-factor sign-in helps, but attackers have learned to wear people down. What the pattern looks like and what to do.
posts.content:
Multi-factor authentication stops most password theft. It does not stop a person who is tired, distracted or simply annoyed. In an MFA fatigue attack, someone who already has a password sends prompt after prompt to the real owner, hoping that one will be approved just to make it stop.

How it shows up on the desk

A run of failed or unanswered prompts, often late in the evening or early in the morning, followed by a sign-in from a country the person has never visited. Our monitoring flags the burst of prompts, and an analyst looks before the next one is sent.

What helps

  • Tell staff that an unexpected prompt is a warning, never a nuisance, and that they should report it
  • Use number matching or app-based prompts instead of plain approve buttons
  • Never approve a prompt you did not start, even if the caller on the phone sounds like IT

If you are a client and a prompt arrives that nobody expects, call the incident line. We would much rather hear about ten false alarms than miss one real one. The desk can disable the account, force a password change and check what the attacker saw, all before the working day begins.

A calm reply and a quick call are worth more than any tool.

posts.title: Leaving staff and forgotten accounts
posts.excerpt: Old accounts are quiet doors. A short leaver checklist closes most of them.
posts.content:
When someone leaves a small firm, the laptop comes back and the email is switched off. The shared spreadsheet login, the supplier portal, the old VPN account and the mailbox forwarding rule usually stay exactly as they were.

These forgotten accounts matter because nobody is watching them, including the person they belonged to. An attacker who finds one has a quiet way in that looks like normal use.

A leaver checklist

  • Disable the sign-in on the last day, rather than deleting it, so you can still see what happened
  • Remove the person from shared mailboxes, shared drives and group chats
  • Check for mail forwarding rules and for apps the person had approved
  • Change any shared passwords the person knew
  • Collect devices, and wipe or reassign them

And for joiners

Start with the least access that does the job and add more when asked. It is much easier than taking things away later.

On the desk we watch for sign-ins to accounts that should be dormant. Often it is a harmless automatic sync. Occasionally it is not, and the note in your monthly report will say which. If you are not sure who still has access to what, ask Priya Nair to include an account review in your next visit.

posts.title: What our monthly report says
posts.excerpt: A look inside the monthly report: what is in it, what is left out on purpose, and how to read it in five minutes.
posts.content:
Every client gets a monthly report. It is written by a person, checked by Ruth Halvorsen and aimed at someone who is not a security specialist. A good one fits on a few pages and takes about five minutes.

What is in it

  • How many alerts we looked at, and how many were closed as harmless
  • The few that mattered, each with what happened and what we did
  • Changes we noticed: new devices, new admin accounts, backups that failed
  • One or two things we recommend you do, in order of importance

Most months the honest summary is that we looked at a lot, closed almost all of it and found nothing that needed your time. We say so. A report that always found something would be suspicious in itself.

What is left out

Jargon, charts for their own sake and fear. If a number is in the report, we can tell you what it means and what, if anything, to do about it.

Watch & Respond and Partner clients also have a quarterly call to talk through the last three months. If you would like to see a sample report before you decide on anything, ask the office and we will send one with the names removed.

posts.title: Before you sign: questions to ask any security provider
posts.excerpt: Eight plain questions that tell you more than any brochure, whoever you choose.
posts.content:
Choosing a security provider is difficult if you are not a specialist. These questions work with us and with anyone else, and the answers matter more than the logo on the proposal.

Questions to ask

  • Who looks at an alert, a person or only software, and at what hour?
  • What was your median time from alert to a person looking at it last year?
  • What can your analysts actually do on my systems, and who decides?
  • Can I see a sample report with the names removed?
  • What does it cost in total, including onboarding and any extra hours?
  • How long is the contract and how do I leave?
  • What happens to my data if we part ways?
  • Which clients are like me, and can I speak to one?

Be careful with anyone who promises that nothing will ever happen, who leads with fear, or who cannot give you a straight number. We never claim zero incidents, and you should not believe a firm that does.

For the record, our answers: a person, around the clock; 11 minutes last year; contain at any hour on Watch & Respond or Partner; yes; the prices on our plans page plus a one-off onboarding fee of EUR 900; 12 months, then month to month with 60 days' notice.
